source: Lakatos (1963) Proofs and Refutations (I), Brit. J. Phil. Sci. 14(53):1-25
finding: Founding text. Uses a classroom dialogue on Euler's polyhedron conjecture (V - E + F = 2) to show that mathematics grows by conjecture, proof, then counterexample, then repair of conjecture, proof or concepts. Part I has sections: problem and conjecture; proof; local-but-not-global counterexamples; global counterexamples (surrender, monster-barring, exception-barring, monster-adjustment, lemma-incorporation).
numbers: Pages 1-25. Written 1958-59, read in Popper's seminar March 1959, circulated mimeographed, then in the 1961 Cambridge PhD thesis. Dedicated to Polya (75th) and Popper (60th birthdays).
quote: We now have at least three opportunities for counterexamples instead of one!
limits: Rational reconstruction with invented speakers (Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta). Not an empirical study. Only Part I was read; sections 5-6 (Parts II-III) were not.
agent_relevance: Decomposing a conjecture into lemmas through its proof gives more places to attack it. A scaffold can ask for a proof sketch first, then test each lemma separately.

source: Lakatos (1963) Proofs and Refutations (I), section 3
finding: Distinguishes a counterexample to a lemma that is local only (attacks one proof step, not the conjecture) from one that is global (attacks the conjecture). In the dialogue, a hollow cube refutes the first lemma (removing a face leaves a plane network) while the conjecture still stands in a repaired form; Gamma attacks the third lemma (triangle removal removes either one edge or two edges and a vertex).
numbers: Three lemmas in Cauchy-style proof: (1) remove a face and stretch flat; (2) triangulate; (3) remove triangles one by one until one remains.
limits: Historical reconstruction of Cauchy 1813 and later critics.
agent_relevance: A failed check should be located: is it the claim that fails, or a step of the proof? G2 (revise from the actual failing output) already says this. Lakatos gives the two-way split: local failure means repair the proof, global failure means repair the claim.

source: Lakatos (1963) Proofs and Refutations (I), section 4 (b)
finding: Names the monster-barring move: reject the counterexample by redefining the key concept so the case is no longer an instance. The picture-frame polyhedron has V - E + F = 0. Alpha presents it as a counterexample; Delta replies it should not be called a polyhedron. Alpha: no hypothesis could not be saved from falsification with a suitable linguistic trick.
numbers: Picture-frame (Fig. 9): V - E + F = 0, not 2.
quote: I look for order and harmony in mathematics, but you only propagate anarchy and chaos.
limits: Dialogue. The move is often a legitimate concept refinement, not always a dodge.
agent_relevance: A model can save a claim by quietly redefining a term. Guard: when a counterexample is rejected, the program should require the reason to be stated as an explicit new definition and re-test all earlier cases against it (G3).

source: Lakatos (1963) Proofs and Refutations (I), contents and section 4 (c)-(e)
finding: Lists the full repertoire of responses to a counterexample: surrender; monster-barring; exception-barring (piecemeal exclusions, strategic withdrawal); monster-adjustment; lemma-incorporation, which turns the proof-generated condition into part of the theorem (proof-generated theorem versus naive conjecture). The contents page names the distinction between monster-barring and monster-adjustment as owed to a colleague (acknowledgement note, not read in detail).
numbers: Five named responses in section 4: (a) surrender, (b) monster-barring, (c) exception-barring, (d) monster-adjustment, (e) lemma-incorporation.
limits: Taxonomy is from one case (Euler). Later claims that it generalises rest on other historical cases, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Gives a closed menu of repair operators when a conjecture is falsified. The schema could use it as an operator list for S5 REVISE on conjecture-type tasks. It is untested.

source: Lakatos (1963) Proofs and Refutations (I), historical footnotes on heuristic order
finding: Claims that conjectures precede proofs in the heuristic order, as in ancient analysis over synthesis. Cites Proclus and Pappus: a theorem is stated first and then demonstrated. Euler in 1750 checked the conjecture on many cases before a proof was found.
numbers: Euler first noted the relation in 1750; proof proposed 1751; Cauchy proof 1813.
limits: Historical claim, argued with quotations, not data.
agent_relevance: Supports a conjecture-then-test loop (guess, check on cases, then prove) instead of proof-first.

source: Rosli, Capraro and Capraro (2014) The effects of problem posing on student mathematical learning: a meta-analysis. Int. Education Studies 7(13):227-241
finding: Pooled 14 datasets (13 studies, 1989-2011) of problem-posing interventions. Gives large positive effects on four outcome types. Says many included studies used Brown and Walter's What-If-Not in class, others used Stoyanova and Ellerton's free, semi-structured and structured posing situations.
numbers: About 1,316 participants (1,038 in grades 3-12, 278 preservice teachers). Initial pool 3,730 works. Hedges g: knowledge/achievement 1.31 (95% CI 1.04-1.59, 4 effects); skill/problem solving 0.83 (.58-1.08, 5); ability/problems posed 0.77 (.57-.98, 7); attitude 0.76 (.59-.93, 6). 11 quasi-experimental, 2 pre-post. Q for knowledge = 68.12 (df 3, p<.001).
limits: Small k. Quasi-experimental. Six studies used researcher-made instruments. Heterogeneity high for knowledge, ability and attitude; moderator tests showed publication source mattered. Effects of 0.8-1.3 are far larger than typical education effects and suggest bias or weak controls. Fixed-effect moderator tests.
agent_relevance: Human evidence that posing helps learning, but it is about students learning, not about an expert solver improving answers. It does not show that posing helps a model answer a given question.

source: Kul and Celik (2020) A meta-analysis of the impact of problem posing strategies on students' learning of mathematics. Rev. Romaneasca pentru Educatie Multidimensionala 12(3):341-368
finding: Random-effects meta-analysis of 20 experimental studies (2000-2020), 31 effect sizes. Effects positive on all four outcome groups. Publication status moderated ability-based effects.
numbers: N = 2,349 students (1,091 experimental, 1,258 control). Random-effects ES: skill-based 1.328 (k=7), ability-based 1.152 (k=5; 95% CI .192-2.113), knowledge-based 1.142 (k=12; Q=123.665), attitude-belief 0.643 (k=7; CI .419-.867). Study type (published vs unpublished) moderated ability-based effects, Qb = 50.028, p<.05. Funnel plot and fail-safe N reported no publication bias.
limits: High heterogeneity (Q=123.665 for knowledge). A published vs unpublished split with Qb=50 undercuts the 'no bias' claim. All ability-based studies used researcher-made tests. Wide CIs.
agent_relevance: Same caution as a06: large pooled effects, high heterogeneity, likely inflated. Treat as weak support.

source: Putra, Herman and Sumarmo (2020) The impact of scientific approach and What-If-Not strategy utilization towards students' mathematical problem posing ability. Int. J. Instruction 13(1):669-684
finding: Pretest-posttest control-group study of What-If-Not combined with a scientific-approach lesson sequence (SA-WIN) versus conventional teaching, grade XI, Cimahi, Indonesia. SA-WIN group gained more on a problem-posing test.
numbers: N = 68 (34 vs 34), 2 intact classes chosen from 8. Posttest mean 24.91 (SD 6.92, 51.9% of ideal) vs 18.06 (SD 5.31, 37.6%); pretest 10.12 vs 10.15 (about 21% both). N-gain 0.40 (SD 0.15) vs 0.21 (SD 0.09), p<0.01. By prior math ability: high 0.59 vs 0.34; medium 0.37 vs 0.20; low 0.31 vs 0.16.
limits: Two classes, not randomised students. WIN is bundled with the scientific approach, so the effect of WIN alone is not isolated. Even the SA-WIN group scored only 52% of ideal on posing. Outcome is posing ability, not solving ability.
agent_relevance: The only WIN-specific numbers opened so far: trained students pose better, but gains are moderate and confounded.

source: Unknown authors (2020) The effects of problem posing learning model on students' learning achievement and motivation. arXiv:2002.04447
finding: Quasi-experiment on cubes and cuboids: the problem-posing model gave no significant gain in achievement but a significant gain in motivation, including interest, enthusiasm, diligence, collaboration and self-control.
numbers: N = 44 (20 experimental, 24 control). No test statistics are given on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract page only was read. Tiny sample. This is a failed or null result on achievement, against the large pooled effects in a06 and a07.
agent_relevance: A counterweight: posing may help attitude more than achievement.

source: Dong and Ma (2025) STP: self-play LLM theorem provers with iterative conjecturing and proving. arXiv:2502.00212
finding: One LLM plays conjecturer and prover. The conjecturer is retrained on conjectures that the current prover can barely prove, so difficulty rises as the prover improves. Reports that this beats plain expert iteration on Lean and Isabelle.
numbers: Lean: 51.3B tokens generated in training; proves 28.5% of LeanWorkbook statements versus 13.2% best prior (expert iteration). Final model: miniF2F-test 65.0% pass@3200, ProofNet-test 23.9% pass@3200, PutnamBench 8/644 at pass@3200 (7/644 at pass@128). 3.6M generated conjectures overall.
limits: Formal Lean/Isabelle statements only. Compute is large. Gains are on training-set coverage plus benchmarks. Training of weights, not a prompt scaffold.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that machine problem posing can pay. But it works by weight updates over many iterations, which our no-training agent cannot copy. The usable idea is selecting conjectures by difficulty relative to the solver.

source: Dong and Ma (2025) STP, reward design for the conjecturer
finding: Conjecture selection rule. Keep a conjecture only if the prover's empirical pass rate over K proofs is in (0, 1/4] and the proof uses the seed lemma. Drop the 20% of conjectures with the lowest minimum-proof-length / statement-length ratio (an elegance filter against artificially complicated goals). Re-weight by Wasserstein distance toward the unproved statements to keep topic diversity. Prover data keep proofs of statements with pass rate below 1/2.
numbers: Pass-rate band (0, 1/4]; elegance filter cuts lowest 20%; prover replay buffer holds the last 3 iterations.
limits: Thresholds are tuned choices with no sensitivity study opened here.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete code-side filter: pass rate strictly between 0 and a low cap, plus a shortness-of-statement filter. Matches G5 (code selects) and G8 (judge by running).

source: Dong and Ma (2025) STP, ablation on training signal
finding: Explains why posing helps: sparse reward. On unproved dataset statements almost no proof attempt succeeds, while generated conjectures are often provable. Retraining on generated conjectures also adds a small gain on external benchmarks.
numbers: At a checkpoint with 11.4% cumulative pass rate on LeanWorkbook (Isabelle), only 131 of 2.5M proofs for the 79K unproved statements were correct. In STP at least 47% of generated conjectures were proved. Final retraining with the conjectures gave about 2-3% gain at pass@128 on miniF2F-test and ProofNet-test.
limits: Isabelle checkpoint. The 2-3% gain is read from the text, not tested across seeds.
agent_relevance: Posing intermediate problems turns near-zero feedback into usable feedback. For an inference-time agent, this is the argument for subgoals that sit just inside the solver's reach (G12: search only where there is a foothold).

source: Poesia, Broman, Haber and Goodman (2024) Learning formal mathematics from intrinsic motivation (Minimo). arXiv:2407.00695
finding: Agent starts from axioms only, in propositional logic, arithmetic and group theory (Peano environment), and learns to conjecture and prove. Uses constrained decoding and type-directed synthesis, so conjectures are well formed even from a random model. Targets hard-but-provable conjectures, using proof-likelihood percentiles to define hard and trivial.
numbers: Conjecture rejection rate under 10% of generations. Initially only about 10-20% of conjectures are proven. Hard = least likely 10% of proofs; trivial = most likely 50%. Group theory: mean proof length 2.67 steps (iteration 1) to 5 (iteration 4); hard conjectures 3.67 to 6.10; longest 4 to 9. Logic: mean 2.75 to 4.21, longest 5 to 11. Arithmetic: mean 2.36 to 3.35, longest 4 to 7. 3 seeds.
limits: Small theories with fixed library (no lemma reuse), so cut-free proofs grow long. Authors state this blocks deep theories. Proof lengths of 3-10 steps are tiny.
agent_relevance: Shows self-posed difficulty can track ability. Also shows the ceiling: without lemma accumulation, posing stalls on small problems.

source: Poesia et al. (2024) Minimo, hindsight relabeling ablation
finding: Without hindsight relabeling, the conjecturer collapses to easy conjectures. With it, failed proof searches still yield true statements (with proofs) that train the conjecturer.
numbers: Compared over 5 iterations in all 3 domains, 3 seeds (standard error bands). Without hindsight, provable conjectures end with high log-likelihood (easy) and do not leave that regime. With it, each batch gives hundreds of true statements from the 80-90% of conjectures not proven directly. Appendix: in arithmetic, without hindsight the provable fraction rises sharply because conjectures become trivial (for example 0 = 0).
limits: Result shown mainly in figures. Exact percentages not read from a table.
agent_relevance: Failure mode to guard against: a self-posing loop drifts to trivial statements. A code-side triviality check (G5) is required.

source: Poesia et al. (2024) Minimo, transfer to human-written theorems
finding: Tests whether the self-trained agent proves human-written theorems it never saw: 35 propositional-logic theorems from Kleene's Introduction to Metamathematics (Theorem 41) and levels of the Natural Number Game that need only axioms.
numbers: 35 Kleene theorems; 10 Natural Number Game levels satisfy the axioms-only criterion. Exact solve rates by iteration were not extracted from the text read.
limits: Numbers for solve rate not recorded here. Test sets are small.
agent_relevance: Transfer to human problems is the real test of posing. The test set is tiny, so treat as suggestive.

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer: automatic generation of mathematical conjectures for theorem proving. arXiv:2506.22005
finding: Rule-based context extraction from Mathlib files plus LLM statement generation, iterated up to 15 times. Funnel from generated to valid to novel to non-trivial conjectures.
numbers: 40 Mathlib seed files. 12,289 conjectures generated; 10,950 parse in Lean 4; 4,130 not already in Mathlib; 3,776 not provable by aesop (non-trivial). Average 103.25 novel conjectures per seed file. 25 of 40 files hit the 15-iteration cap. The prompt phrase 'as many as possible' kept volume steady.
limits: Only about 31% of generated statements survive as novel and non-trivial (3,776 / 12,289). Novel means absent from Mathlib, not interesting.
agent_relevance: Realistic yield of unguided conjecture generation: roughly one in three after code filters. Plan budget for it.

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer, GRPO on generated conjectures
finding: Reinforcement learning (GRPO) on DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B using 192 generated topology conjectures raised per-proof success but barely raised the number of distinct problems solved. Authors note gains may not generalise to new problem types in the same domain.
numbers: Per-proof success: DSP-V1.5-RL 982/24576; DSP-V2-7B 2285/24576; +GRPO 1 epoch 2306/24576; +GRPO 10 epochs 3657/24576 (16 hours). Problems solved: 43, 47, 48, 49 of 192. Later text: proofs 2285 to 5307, problems 47 to 50 of 192. Alpha-open set test: 443/1792 proofs and 9/14 problems after 1 epoch; 454/1792 and 8/14 after 10 epochs.
limits: One domain (topology), one seed, no variance. The gain is per-attempt reliability, not coverage. Generated conjectures can also repeat a pattern: when proved theorems were in context the model tended to repeat similar patterns.
agent_relevance: A cautionary result: more proofs of the same posed problems is not more problems solved. Same as the plateau seen in a12.

source: Kasaura et al. (2026) Discovering new theorems via LLMs with in-context proof learning in Lean (Conjecturing-Proving Loop). arXiv:2509.14274
finding: Conjecturing-Proving Loop (CPL): propose a conjecture in Lean 4, check syntax and novelty with exact?, try to prove, and put verified theorems and proofs into the next prompt. Compared with simultaneous generation of statement and proof (SL). CPL found a hard target theorem; SL never did.
numbers: o3 as conjecturer and prover; 14M-token API budget per run; 20 runs each. Target (intersection of two alpha-open sets is alpha-open): found 5/20 for CPL, 0/20 for SL (Fisher exact p = 0.024). CPL generated 106 theorems per run on average, SL 328. CPL proofs were longer (Kolmogorov-Smirnov p = 1e-13).
limits: One target theorem, one model, one topology domain. Fisher p = 0.024 from 5 versus 0 successes is fragile. Target found only after about 49 theorems on average.
agent_relevance: Posing separately from proving, plus keeping verified results in context, found a hard result that joint generation missed. This is a no-training method our agent could use.

source: Kasaura et al. (2026) CPL, in-context learning check
finding: Context of earlier verified theorems makes the prover better, even when those theorems are not used as lemmas.
numbers: Re-proving all 2,123 CPL theorems: 99% (2106) with generated library in context versus 91% (1935) with only definitions (McNemar p = 4e-35). Target theorem re-proved 7 times in 80 tries (5 contexts x 16) with library, 0/80 without. Without library, GPT-4o called the true proposition false 10 times and gave wrong proofs 6 times (on the natural-language attempt).
limits: The 2,123 theorems were generated under the same context, so re-proof may be easier than first proof. The proof did not use the other generated theorems as lemmas.
agent_relevance: Worked examples in context help the prover on related statements. Supports keeping a short log of verified findings (S9) in context.

source: Chuharski, Rojas Collins and Meringolo (2024) Mining math conjectures from LLMs: a pruning approach. arXiv:2412.16177
finding: Lakatos-style loop in code: LLMs (GPT-4, Claude Sonnet, Gemini 1.5) propose conjectures about the solubilizer in group theory and write GAP code to find counterexamples. A conjecture survives if no counterexample is found in the groups tried. An expert on the solubilizer literature checked all 420 unique outputs.
numbers: 757 outputs, 420 unique (55.5% unique). Counterexamples found for 109 (25.95%). Only 40 (9.52%) survived with no counterexample. Valid share: GPT-4 26.60%, Gemini 4.64%, Claude 4.49%. 64.52% (271) of outputs had non-executable GAP code (Gemini 81.86%, Claude 49.44%, GPT-4 37.76%).
limits: No counterexample in tested groups is not a proof. Most surviving GPT-4 conjectures concerned the size of the solubilizer, an easy target. Authors call the results 'not groundbreaking'. One prompt-leak duplicate (a known theorem in the system prompt).
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that posing then falsifying by execution works but with low yield (under 10% survive). Counterexample search needs code that runs; a third of runs failed here.

source: Chuharski et al. (2024), OpenAI o1 side result
finding: A small extra run with o1 gave much better yield and code reliability than GPT-4, Claude and Gemini.
numbers: 51 conjectures, all unique. 22 had no counterexample (43%), 28 failed (55%), 1 could not execute code (about 98% executed). Authors say the sample is too small for strong claims.
limits: Appendix, 51 samples, not finished by authors.
agent_relevance: Suggests a stronger reasoning model improves the surviving fraction. Needs a larger sample.

source: Sivakumar, Borchert, Cardenas and Lampouras (2025) Conjecturing: an overlooked step in formal mathematical reasoning. arXiv:2510.11986
finding: Many problems ('find the minimum number', 'prove or disprove') need a conjectured answer before they can be formalised. ConjectureBench tests conjecturing alone and inside autoformalisation, with GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek-V3.1. Autoformalisation scores are inflated when the answer is given.
numbers: 457 problems: numerical 178, algebraic 165, proof 114. Standalone conjecture equivalence (equiv rfl) pass@1/pass@10: GPT-4.1 3.28/5.04% (15/457, 23/457); DeepSeek-V3.1 3.72/5.70% (17/457, 26/457). Proof type 0/114 and 1/114. Autoformalisation Grader@10 falls from 36.32% (seen conjecture) to 20.35% (unseen) for GPT-4.1 baseline, and 35.67% to 24.95% for DeepSeek-V3.1 baseline. Judge pass@1 for LEAN-FIRE: GPT-4.1 78.77 seen vs 26.70 unseen (w/o few-shot) ; DeepSeek 92.78 vs 55.80.
limits: Standalone equiv rfl is a strict, exact-match metric, so true ability is higher than 3-6%. Signs of data contamination found (IsMagicSquare helper). LEAN-FIRE gain came mostly from few-shot examples, not the hybrid reasoning. Table layout is hard to read in the text extraction, so the model-row assignment of Table 3 is partly inferred.
agent_relevance: The model often does not state the conjecture explicitly. Make the program force a separate explicit conjecture step, and check it against code before trusting a downstream answer.

source: Sivakumar et al. (2025) ConjectureBench, headline results for LEAN-FIRE
finding: Inference-time method LEAN-FIRE interleaves chain-of-thought with Lean steps. It achieves the first end-to-end formalisation of some PutnamBench problems. Authors conclude that models have the knowledge but treat conjecturing as part of memorised complete solutions.
numbers: 13 PutnamBench problems formalised end to end with GPT-4.1 and 7 with DeepSeek-V3.1. Average ConJudge gain 29.1% (GPT-4.1) and 14.0% (DeepSeek-V3.1). Standalone performance is nearly an order of magnitude lower than conjecturing inside autoformalisation.
limits: Few-shot examples, not the method, gave the main benefit (w/o few-shot drops sharply). Contamination signs.
agent_relevance: Isolating the conjecture as its own scored slot exposes a hidden weakness that end-to-end scores hide.

source: Xu, Jin, Arya and Naik (2026) MathDuels: a self-play benchmark that grows (COLM 2026). arXiv:2604.21916
finding: 19 frontier models both author and solve problems. A Rasch model estimates solver ability and problem difficulty jointly. Authoring and solving are only partly the same skill: the best solver (GPT-5.4-high) is not the best author (Gemini-3.1-Pro-high, whose problems have the lowest solve rate, 62.9%). Newcomers' problems beat the previous top solvers more often.
numbers: 30 problems per model, 570 total, 11 excluded, 559 valid, 10,062 solve observations. 39% of valid problems solved by every non-author solver. Of 275 problems by the two newest models, 27.6% (76/275) defeat at least one prior top-3 solver, versus 8.0% (165/2054) for the rest. Ratings: Gemini-3.1-Pro-high solver 2214, author 1624, composite 1919; GPT-5.4-high solver 2268, author 1473, composite 1870. Mean rank range 5.05 of 19 at k=30. Temperature 1.0.
limits: Authors are asked for problems with one checkable answer (math-verify). Verification used GPT-5.4-high, a model from the field. An author's difficulty is partly ill-posedness. Bootstrapped CIs overlap widely in the middle.
agent_relevance: Good posing is a separate skill from solving. Do not assume that a strong solver is also good at posing. Measure it.

source: Xu et al. (2026) MathDuels, pipeline ablation
finding: Harder problem authoring doubles the error rate of invalid or wrong-key problems. Each added pipeline stage (meta-prompting, difficulty amplification) increases errors. Code execution at solve time only lowers it a little.
numbers: 432 model-pair observations per setting. Errors without code: 1-step 22 (5.1%), 2-step 41 (9.5%), 3-step 108 (25.0%). With code execution: 13 (3.0%), 30 (6.9%), 91 (21.1%). With code at authoring time: 84 (21.8%).
limits: Errors here include both author mistakes and solver mistakes. The table text layout was partly reconstructed.
agent_relevance: Pushing a model to pose harder problems makes the posed problem wrong about one time in four at the top tier. Every posed problem must be verified before it is used (G3, G8).

source: Brown and Walter (1983/2005) The Art of Problem Posing; What-if-not? An elaboration and second illustration (1970)
finding: Source of the What-If-Not method: list the attributes of a given statement or problem, then negate or vary each attribute and ask what the new problem would be. Known here only through citations in a06 and a08, and the ERIC records (ED251290, EJ025805).
numbers: Not read. The ERIC listing shows a 1970 article and the 1983 book (2005 third edition cited in a06).
limits: Book not opened. Original steps (choosing a starting point, listing attributes, what-if-not, question asking, analysis) are not verified from the source this session.
agent_relevance: The method is a code-driven operator: attribute list, then systematic negation, then test of each variant. Easy to turn into a scaffold step, but needs reading the primary text first.

source: ERIC records on WIN studies (2018): Effectiveness of What if Not strategy with dynamic geometry software (EJ1186756); What if Not strategy for open-ended problem posing in inquiry-based geometry class (EJ1301417)
finding: Two further studies pair WIN with geometry. Only the titles were seen in the ERIC search listing. Full text was not available from the ERIC full-text link.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened. Listed only so the next pass can open them.
agent_relevance: Candidate sources for WIN-specific evidence in geometry.
